claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially a single-phase, high-temperature BCC alloy.
Phase stability during cooling is governed primarily by the composition-dependent free-energy difference between BCC and FCC phases.
Al content modulates the free-energy difference between the competing phases.
The Al content in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 stabilizes BCC at elevated temperatures.
Cooling reduces the configurational-entropy contribution that stabilizes the high-temperature BCC phase.
Cooling increases the chemical driving force for phase separation.
At lower temperatures, thermodynamic changes favor transformation from BCC to FCC and/or B2.
Atomic-size and electronic effects produce an enthalpic preference for FCC and/or B2 over BCC.
The onset and extent of transformation are determined primarily by BCC thermodynamic instability relative to FCC/B2 rather than by kinetic barriers.
Cooling rate affects the scale of phase separation but not the fundamental phase stability.
Slow cooling will cause partial or complete transformation of BCC to FCC and/or B2.
Formation of FCC and/or B2 will produce new diffraction peaks and microstructural features.
Rapid water quenching will retain more BCC than furnace cooling.
A sufficiently large thermodynamic driving force may permit incipient transformation even during rapid quenching.
The transformation temperature will correlate with the calculated free-energy difference between BCC and FCC/B2.
The extent of phase separation will correlate with the calculated free-energy difference between BCC and FCC/B2.
The proposed mechanism applies to Cr-Co-Fe-Ni-Al alloys near 7 at.% Al with similarly high Cr content.
The mechanism may not apply at substantially lower or higher Al contents, with significant impurities, or from different initial microstructures.
Kinetic factors and minor composition variations may alter the transformation temperature and phase fractions.
